title: Ellipsoidal Time Series Forecasting
claim: The learned local spectral structure reproduces the true chaotic attractor's geometry and exposes interpretable stability information along the trajectory.
layout: 2 side-by-side 3D panels, left-to-right, matched axes with colorbars
description: Two side-by-side 3D line plots of the Lorenz-63 butterfly attractor under the shared title 'Attractor Reconstruction (Side-by-Side)'. The left panel, 'Ground Truth (Color: Speed)', draws the trajectory in a blue gradient. Light blue marks slow regions near the center and dark blue marks fast regions on the outer lobes. The right panel, 'Prediction (Color: Eigen Max)', draws the model's reconstructed trajectory in an orange-to-brown gradient. Light orange marks low maximum eigenvalues near the lobe crossover and dark brown marks high values on the outer loops. Both panels use identical x, y and z axes with gridded 3D boxes, and each has a vertical colorbar on its right. The two double-lobed shapes closely match, so the eye compares the lobes and the color patterns.
caption: Lorenz-63 attractor reconstruction with \Fern. Left: ground-truth trajectory colored by instantaneous speed (norm of velocity). Right: \Fern\ prediction, colored by the mean patch-wise maximum eigenvalue (spectral radius of the local SPD map).
abstract: We argue that long-term forecasting requires learning local Jacobians with explicit spectral structure, going beyond simple conditional mean matching. Our method, Fern, invokes Brenier's theorem to directly parameterize the Jacobian as a symmetric positive semi-definite (SPD) factorization, treating forecasting as the optimal transport of probability mass from a fixed Gaussian source to data-dependent ellipsoids. This formulation reduces the computational cost of eigendecomposition from cubic to linear time while providing interpretable, geometry-aware projections. To rigorously evaluate robustness, we introduce a synthetic benchmark with controlled non-stationary shocks alongside new metrics like Effective Prediction Time (EPT). Fern demonstrates exceptional stability, outperforming baselines like DLinear and Koopa by over two orders of magnitude (up to 790x) on nonstationary settings where standard benchmarks fail to expose model brittleness.
